builder_plan.scenario: Your coding assistant makes changes that still need substantial repair before merging.
builder_plan.change: Try the technique on held-out issues from a repository with reliable tests.
builder_plan.baseline: The same coding agent, repository snapshot, tools, and token budget.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Correct patches, regression failures, human repair time, and total cost per accepted change.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: SmartLens: Turning AI Agent Changes into Learning, Review, and Risk Signals in the IDE
summary: SmartLens replaces manual diff-by-diff review of AI agent output with IDE-side attribution of pending changes to agent, developer, or both, plus skill-gap analysis and risk-ranked review prioritization built on Git history. It costs little in infrastructure (an IDE plugin, no model training or GPU), but adds workflow complexity and depends on instrumented attribution of agent edits, which has known blind spots where attribution fails. After adoption, misattribution can silently misdirect review priority and risk rankings, and the claimed bug-fix prediction advantage may degrade since part of it stems from recency rather than the risk signal itself.
rationale: The technique targets a real gap (attributing pending AI-agent edits for review prioritization), but the evaluation is preliminary, tool-specific (IntelliJ), and its risk-prediction advantage over churn is partially confounded by recency, so it warrants a small-scale trial rather than production adoption.
technique: IDE plugin attributing AI-agent code changes

claims.statement: SmartLens replaces manual diff-by-diff review of AI agent output with IDE-side attribution of pending changes to agent, developer, or both, plus skill-gap analysis and risk-ranked review prioritization built on Git history. It costs little in infrastructure (an IDE plugin, no model training or GPU), but adds workflow complexity and depends on instrumented attribution of agent edits, which has known blind spots where attribution fails. After adoption, misattribution can silently misdirect review priority and risk rankings, and the claimed bug-fix prediction advantage may degrade since part of it stems from recency rather than the risk signal itself.

Correctly attributed changes in 8 of 12 scripted IDE scenarios; risk ranking was as good as or better than plain code churn at predicting later bug fixes, though part of the gain is attributable to recency effects.
